**4B.9 Research Note**
Kishida’s 2024 record does not show use of surveillance, internet shutdowns, or digital repression to narrow political freedom. The strongest evidence is on the opposite side: legalistic cyber-defense work, fact-checking/provenance tools, and anti-disinformation governance. The only real negatives I found are structural, especially Japan’s preexisting media/self-censorship pressures, not clear 2024 coercion by Kishida.

- [Kishida says Japan will enhance security clearances and cyber security and accelerate a bill to build the domestic legal structure](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202401/30shiseihoshin.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | January 30, 2024 | Kishida framed security-clearance and cyber-security legislation as formal legal preparation and risk management. This is relevant because it shows institutionalization, not discretionary surveillance abuse. | Question IDs: 4B.9

- [Kishida convenes expert panel on active cyber defense legislation](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/actions/202406/07cyber.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | June 7, 2024 | Kishida asked a 17-expert panel to shape active cyber-defense bills. The source presents the process as expert-led and legal, which cuts against a claim of covert digital repression. | Question IDs: 4B.9

- [Kishida warns generative AI can spread disinformation and calls for trustworthy AI](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202405/02ai.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | May 2, 2024 | Kishida explicitly treated AI-generated disinformation as a governance problem and backed provenance verification. This supports a pro-information-integrity reading rather than censorship or propaganda. | Question IDs: 4B.9; 4B.6

- [The Importance of Fact-Checking in the Digital Era](https://www.japan.go.jp/kizuna/2024/01/growing_importance_of_fact-checking.html) | JapanGov / Government of Japan | January 26, 2024 | The government page quotes Kishida saying technologies that prove and confirm information origin are effective for reliable information distribution. This is direct evidence of support for information access and verification tools. | Question IDs: 4B.9; 4B.6

- [Third Summit for Democracy: Technology, Elections and Mis-/Dis-information](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/diplomatic/202403/20democracy.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | March 20, 2024 | Kishida participated in a session focused on mis/disinformation and elections, which is consistent with concern about information integrity rather than political surveillance. I found no indication in this source of coercive digital control. | Question IDs: 4B.9; 4B.6

- [Japan: Freedom on the Net 2024](https://freedomhouse.org/country/japan/freedom-net/2024) | Freedom House | 2024 | Freedom House says Japan does not typically block or filter content, but notes government pressure and the kisha kurabu system can contribute to self-censorship and restricted access. This is the main negative structural evidence, though it is not Kishida-specific repression in 2024. | Question IDs: 4B.9; 4B.6

- [Japan: Freedom in the World 2024](https://freedomhouse.org/country/japan/freedom-world/2024) | Freedom House | 2024 | Freedom House rates Japan free and says the government generally operates with openness and transparency, while media freedoms remain constrained by press-club access limits. This is mixed evidence, but it still does not show Kishida using administrative harassment to suppress political freedom. | Question IDs: 4B.9; 4B.6

- [Digital News Report 2024: Japan](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2024/japan) | Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism | June 17, 2024 | The report describes Japan’s media as competitive but under pressure from declining revenues, disinformation concerns, and the need for fact-checking and provenance tools. It supports a fragile-information-environment reading, not a repression reading. | Question IDs: 4B.9; 4B.6

**Search gap**
I found no credible 2024 evidence that Kishida used surveillance, internet shutdowns, or administrative harassment to limit political freedom. The closest material was lawful cyber-defense and information-integrity policy, not repression.
